clue.text: Operatic captain keeping Erica dry?

parts.note: a mac is the raincoat that keeps its wearer dry
Erica is the botanical genus of heather, so it stands for heath

explanation.surface: A question about a stage captain shielding a woman called Erica from the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: Erica looks like a woman's name but is the Latin name for heather, HEATH; a MAC keeps it dry. Captain Macheath is the highwayman hero of The Beggar's Opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Macheath is the dashing highwayman captain in Gay's ballad opera The Beggar's Opera.

clue.text: Something unforeseen.I had found in stress

indicators.note: found in tells us the short form of I had sits inside the word for stress

parts.note: an accent is stress laid on a syllable
I had contracts to I'd, written ID

explanation.surface: Someone confesses that they unexpectedly found themselves under stress.
explanation.definitionFit: A mishap is by nature an unplanned, unexpected event.

clue.text: A cardinal architectural achievement

parts.note: read as the building work of a cardinal: the Thames-side palace built by Cardinal Wolsey and later taken by Henry VIII

explanation.surface: Praise for a prime piece of architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cardinal' reads as 'principal' but means a churchman: Cardinal Wolsey built this palace on the Thames near London.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tudor palace was built for Cardinal Wolsey, a churchman's grand building project.

clue.text: Can be persuaded to have the last word ?

definitions.meaning: describes someone willing to be talked round
read as able to say the final word of a prayer, the closing 'so be it'

explanation.surface: A question about whether someone who likes the last word can ever be talked round.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading splits the word into AMEN, the last word of a prayer, and ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone tractable and responsive yields readily to argument.

clue.text: Many have a high time after her reception

definitions.text: Many have a high time after her reception

parts.words: Many have a high time after her reception
parts.note: read as a woman who welcomes guests to a party, after which they enjoy themselves; or the air stewardess who greets passengers before the flight takes them up high

explanation.surface: A party-giver's guests carry on merrily once her welcome is over.
explanation.definitionFit: She is the woman who receives guests, at a party or aboard an airliner.

clue.text: The beer to follow wallop ?

parts.note: wallop is British slang for beer and also means a hard blow or sting; this strong old ale follows on from it

explanation.surface: A question about which beer to drink after a pint of wallop.
explanation.walkthrough: Wallop is British slang for beer, and a wallop is also a sting; the answer is an old name for strong ale, starting with that sting.
explanation.definitionFit: Stingo is an old English name for strong, well-aged ale.

clue.text: Ain't possible to name her

indicators.note: possible here means one possible rearrangement of the letters of the word before it

explanation.surface: Someone protests that naming her simply cannot be done.
explanation.definitionFit: Tina is a girl's first name, so it is one way to name a woman.

clue.text: Foundation garment fitted doesn't slip'

parts.note: stays are an old-fashioned corset, a foundation garment
put in the sense of placed or fitted in position

explanation.surface: A well-fitted corset doesn't ride down.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that remains in place and refuses to move does not slip.

clue.text: Work, Timothy, it's wrong to be so hopeful

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work

indicators.note: wrong signals that the letters of the word beside it are put in the wrong order

explanation.surface: Someone tells Timothy that hoping for so much is a mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: A hopeful, as a noun, is a person who expects things to turn out well.

clue.text: Riding high, that's the worst of it

definitions.text: Riding high, that's the worst of it

parts.words: Riding high, that's the worst of it
parts.note: read as the froth that floats on top of a liquid, which is also the lowest, worst sort of people

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that the worst part of success is riding high.
explanation.definitionFit: Froth that rises to the surface is refuse, and the word also means the vilest of people.

clue.text: Reformation — style architecture

parts.note: read not as Tudor church history but as a building designed for reforming offenders

explanation.surface: A label for buildings in the style of the Protestant Reformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformation' suggests sixteenth-century church history; it means reforming criminals, and the building is a prison.
explanation.definitionFit: A prison intended to reform its inmates is a building whose purpose is reformation.

clue.text: What went before the Sahib's fall ?

definitions.text: What went before the Sahib's fall

parts.words: What went before the Sahib's fall
parts.note: read as the season before autumn (fall) for an Englishman in India, or the last glory before the Raj ended

explanation.surface: A question about what led up to the downfall of the British in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' is both the downfall of the Raj and the American word for autumn; a warm spell late in the year comes before autumn.
explanation.definitionFit: A spell of warm weather late in the year precedes autumn, and figuratively a late flowering before decline.

clue.text: Drink up again yet may be right sober

indicators.note: may be signals that the letters could be rearranged into another word

explanation.surface: Someone drinking again yet might still be perfectly sober.
explanation.definitionFit: To absorb again is to soak up or take in a liquid a second time.

clue.text: White-headed MP 'seen out in the cold

definitions.text: White-headed MP 'seen out in the cold

parts.words: White-headed MP 'seen out in the cold
parts.note: read not as a grey politician sent out of favour but as a white-flowered plant that blooms in winter

explanation.surface: A grey-haired member of parliament spotted out in the cold, out of favour.
explanation.walkthrough: The MP left 'out in the cold' suggests a politician in disgrace; it is a white-flowered winter bulb.
explanation.definitionFit: This small bulb bears a drooping white flower head and blooms in late winter.

clue.text: Pig-killer, by gum !

definitions.meaning: a pig-..., someone or something that kills pigs by stabbing
a label that holds by means of gum, an adhesive

explanation.surface: An exclamation of surprise about a slaughterer of pigs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By gum!' reads as a northern English exclamation, but means 'by means of glue'.
explanation.definitionFit: A pig-sticker stabs pigs, and an adhesive label clings by its glue.

clue.text: The only gold vouchsafed the poor (Dekker)

definitions.text: The only gold vouchsafed the poor (Dekker)

parts.words: The only gold vouchsafed the poor (Dekker)
parts.note: alludes to Thomas Dekker's lullaby 'Golden ... kiss your eyes': the golden thing the poor get is sleep

explanation.surface: A line about the only riches granted to the poor, credited to the playwright Dekker.
explanation.walkthrough: Dekker's song begins 'Golden slumbers kiss your eyes'; sleep is the only gold the poor are given.
explanation.definitionFit: Sleep, called golden in the Elizabethan song, costs nothing and comes to rich and poor alike.

clue.text: Get wet through, taking Enid for a ride

indicators.note: through tells us the weather word goes right into the middle of the first word

parts.note: rain is wet weather

explanation.surface: Someone gets soaked while out riding with Enid.
explanation.walkthrough: In Tennyson's Idylls of the King, Geraint makes his wife Enid ride before him through the wilds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arthurian knight Geraint, husband of Enid, makes her ride with him to test her loyalty.

clue.text: What about that gadding 'vine of Ronald's?.

indicators.note: gadding means wandering about, so the letters roam into a new order

parts.note: Ron's, the short form of Ronald with its possessive

explanation.surface: A question about Ronald's wandering vine.
explanation.definitionFit: Surroundings are what lies about, or around, a place.

clue.text: On the verge of stinginess ? That's sinister

definitions.meaning: near means stingy, and the side by the verge of the road is the kerbside
sinister is Latin for left, the kerb side of a car in Britain

explanation.surface: Someone close to meanness is called sinister.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain cars drive on the left, so the near side, next to the verge, is the left; 'near' also means mean with money.
explanation.definitionFit: In British driving the side next to the kerb is the left, which is what sinister means in heraldry.

clue.text: What to do for toast — or how to disappoint one's date

definitions.meaning: to rise to one's feet when a toast is drunk
to fail to turn up for an arranged meeting

explanation.surface: Advice on etiquette at a dinner, and on letting a date down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'toast' looks like bread but is the drink to someone's health, for which everyone rises.
explanation.definitionFit: Guests rise to their feet for a toast, and a date who is jilted is left waiting.

clue.text: Aunt Lund madly waving

indicators.note: madly signals that the letters of the two words beside it go wild into a new order

explanation.surface: An aunt called Lund is gesturing wildly.
explanation.definitionFit: Undulant means rising and falling in waves.

clue.text: The jet set

parts.note: read not as rich socialites but literally as the group who fly jet planes

explanation.surface: The fashionable rich who fly around the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilots and aircrew of the air force are the people who fly jets.

clue.text: Such as could make no match, though

definitions.text: Such as could make no match, though

parts.words: Such as could make no match, though
parts.note: a Roman virgin priestess of Vesta could never marry, yet her name is also that of a wax match

explanation.surface: A remark about someone unable to find a partner.
explanation.walkthrough: The priestesses of Vesta were sworn to virginity, so made no marriage match; 'though' points to a vesta also being a match for lighting.
explanation.definitionFit: Vestal virgins, guardians of the Roman sacred fire, were bound to chastity.

clue.text: Before Harfleur this creature's may have preceded the tiger's action

definitions.text: Before Harfleur this creature's may have preceded the tiger's action

parts.words: Before Harfleur this creature's may have preceded the tiger's action
parts.note: alludes to Henry V at the siege of Harfleur, urging his men to imitate the action of the tiger; a siege engine named after a male sheep would have gone first

explanation.surface: Musing on the siege of Harfleur and the King's call to fight like tigers.
explanation.walkthrough: In Shakespeare's Henry V, before Harfleur, the King cries 'imitate the action of the tiger'; the creature here is a ram, whose action, battering, came first.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy beam used to break down walls or gates in sieges, its name taken from a male sheep.

clue.text: A high spot of Continental travel

definitions.meaning: the French word for a tower, a high place on the Continent
a journey round a number of places

explanation.surface: A highlight of a trip around mainland Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Continental' means French here: their word for tower is spelt the same as the English word for a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: In French the word means tower, a lofty structure, and in English a journey visiting several places.

clue.text: As 22 is, and also serves

definitions.meaning: a vestal is a virgin, an unmarried girl
a domestic servant, one who serves

explanation.surface: A cross-reference saying the vestal is also a servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A vestal virgin is an unmarried girl, and a domestic servant waits on others.

clue.text: Two French painters and a writer

definitions.meaning: Henri, the naive painter, and Theodore, the landscape painter, shared the surname
Jean-Jacques, the Geneva-born philosopher and author of The Social Contract

explanation.surface: A list of three famous Frenchmen of the arts.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to painters Henri and Theodore and to the philosopher-author Jean-Jacques.

clue.text: Dad's essays have raised the dough

parts.note: Pa's, a short word for father with its possessive
tries in the sense of attempts, as essays means attempts

explanation.surface: Father's attempts have earned plenty of money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised the dough' suggests making money, but means baked goods made with risen dough; 'essays' means attempts, not compositions.
explanation.definitionFit: Pies and tarts are baked goods made from dough.
